# Florence 1347 – Physics, optics & astronomy

K = knowledge level · use = none/wrong/partial/correct · make = producibility with local means · accept = acceptance.

- **Ground lenses** [`lenses`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/lenses.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Only convex lenses, ground from rock crystal, beryl or greenish glass full of bubbles. Concave lenses and clear cristallo glass do not exist. Local: spectacle makers (the craft began in Pisa or Florence c. 1286; no named Florentine workshop is documented for 1347); glassmakers of Gambassi and the Valdelsa. Elsewhere: Venice, rock-crystal workers (cristallieri) with guild rules on reading glasses since 1300-1301; Murano glassmakers.
- **Spectacles** [`spectacles`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/spectacles.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. About sixty years old and still a marvel: riveted pairs with convex lenses for ageing readers only. Nothing helps the short-sighted. Local: Dominicans of Santa Maria Novella (Giordano da Pisa praised the invention there in 1306); convent of Santa Caterina in Pisa (friar Alessandro della Spina made them, died 1313). Elsewhere: Venice, cristallieri.
- **Law of refraction, image formation and vision** [`refraction_optics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/refraction_optics.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Perspectiva (Alhazen, Witelo, Pecham, Bacon) is read in the friars' schools; no sine law. The crystalline humour is held to be the seat of vision. Local: convent schools of Santa Maria Novella and Santa Croce. Elsewhere: Paris and Oxford arts faculties; papal court at Avignon.
- **Camera obscura** [`camera_obscura`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/camera_obscura.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept high. Known from Alhazen and Pecham as a way to watch solar eclipses through a small hole. Nobody uses a lens in the hole or draws with it. Elsewhere: Provence, Levi ben Gerson (died 1344) observed with a dark chamber; Paris astronomers.
- **Microscope** [`microscope`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/microscope.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept medium. A fused glass bead held in a pierced plate magnifies strongly; spectacle lenses are too weak. Common glass is tinted but a tiny bead is clear enough. Local: glassmakers of Gambassi and the Valdelsa.
- **Telescope (refractor)** [`telescope`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/telescope.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept high. No concave lenses exist. Two convex lenses give an inverted image; the strong eyepiece must be ground specially and the glass is streaky. Local: lens grinders.
- **Reflecting telescope** [`reflecting_telescope`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/reflecting_telescope.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept medium. Bell founders know hard high-tin bronze and burning mirrors are described in perspectiva texts. Nobody can figure a mirror accurately. Local: bell founders.

- **Spectrum and the nature of colour** [`spectrum_colour`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/spectrum_colour.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept medium. Colours are light mixed with darkness (Aristotle). A physician's water-filled urine flask shows the rainbow as Theodoric of Freiberg did; six-sided rock crystals throw colours. - **Waves - sound and light** [`wave_nature_light_sound`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/wave_nature_light_sound.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Boethius teaches sound as struck air spreading like ripples from a stone in water; string ratios are taught as musica. Light as a wave is unknown. Local: organ builders; lute makers. Elsewhere: Paris, Jean de Murs writes on musical proportion.
- **Finite speed of light** [`speed_of_light`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/speed_of_light.md) — K2, use none, make very-hard, accept low. Aristotle treats illumination as instantaneous; Alhazen and Bacon argue that light takes time. No experiment within reach could decide it.
- **Photography** [`photography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/photography.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept low. Aqua fortis to dissolve silver is a rarity of a few alchemists. An image made by light alone smells of sorcery.
- **Lever, pulley, inclined plane (statics)** [`lever_mechanics_statics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/lever_mechanics_statics.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Builders work by rule of thumb; the steelyard is everywhere. Jordanus' science of weights and Moerbeke's Archimedes sit in Latin manuscripts no craftsman reads. Local: Opera del Duomo (campanile works); merchants' steelyards.
- **Buoyancy and hydrostatics** [`buoyancy_hydrostatics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/buoyancy_hydrostatics.md) — K2, use none, make easy, accept high. The crown story is known from a Latin poem on weights; Moerbeke's translation of On Floating Bodies (1269) is very rare. The mint assays by touchstone and fire. Local: the Zecca (mint of the gold florin); goldsmiths.
- **Falling bodies and projectiles** [`falling_bodies`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/falling_bodies.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept low. Aristotle: heavier falls faster, in proportion. Bradwardine's rule (1328) and Heytesbury's mean-speed theorem (1335) are new Oxford arguments, barely known in Italy and never tested. Elsewhere: Oxford, Merton College (Heytesbury, Dumbleton, Swineshead); Paris, Jean Buridan.
- **Laws of motion** [`laws_of_motion`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/laws_of_motion.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept low. Italian schools follow Aristotle and Averroes: the air pushes a thrown stone on. Buridan is teaching impetus in Paris right now. Rest is the natural state. Elsewhere: Paris, Jean Buridan lectures on impetus.
- **Universal gravitation** [`universal_gravitation`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/universal_gravitation.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept low. Heavy things seek the centre of the world, which is the Earth's centre. A force acting across empty space sounds like astrology or magic.
- **Strength of materials and scaling** [`strength_of_materials`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/strength_of_materials.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept high. Masons trust proportion rules and precedent. The new cathedral and bell tower are being built without calculation; breaking test beams and cords is cheap. Local: Opera del Duomo.
- **Sundial and water clock** [`sundial_water_clock`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/sundial_water_clock.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. The day runs by bells for the canonical hours, which stretch and shrink with the season. Equal hours belong to astronomers; dials have no pole-pointing gnomon. Local: bell of the Badia (rings terce and nones); sundials on churches.
- **Mechanical clock (escapement, spring drive)** [`mechanical_clock`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/mechanical_clock.md) — K2, use partial, make hard, accept high. Florence has no public clock (first in 1353). Weight-driven striking clocks in Milan and Padua are admired novelties; a smith needs the verge escapement explained. Local: smiths and bell founders; tower of the Palazzo dei Priori (no clock yet). Elsewhere: Padua, Jacopo Dondi's tower clock (1344); Milan, striking clock of San Gottardo (1336); St Albans, Richard of Wallingford's astronomical clock.
- **Pendulum clock** [`pendulum_clock`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/pendulum_clock.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept high. Needs a working verge clock first, and no clockmaker lives in the city. A pendulum on a tower clock would outdo every clock in Europe.
- **Air pressure and the barometer** [`atmospheric_pressure`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/atmospheric_pressure.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept low. Nature abhors a vacuum, though since 1277 Paris masters allow that God could make one. Needs a yard-long sealed glass tube and mercury. Local: apothecaries (quicksilver); glassmakers of Gambassi; cinnabar mines of Monte Amiata. Elsewhere: Almaden (Spain) mercury mines; Murano glassmakers.
- **Air pump and vacuum experiments** [`air_pump_vacuum`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/air_pump_vacuum.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept low. No piston pumps exist to start from; only clyster syringes. A fitted bronze barrel with valves and thick glass vessels are all new work.
- **Thermometer and temperature scale** [`thermometer_temperature`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/thermometer_temperature.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept medium. Physicians judge fever by touch and pulse; Galenic pharmacy counts four degrees of hot and cold. An open air-and-water thermoscope is easy, a sealed spirit tube harder. Local: glassmakers of Gambassi; apothecaries (aqua vitae).
- **Specific and latent heat** [`latent_specific_heat`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/latent_specific_heat.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept low. Heat and cold are qualities, not quantities. Needs a thermometer first.

Heat is the element fire. Perpetual-motion wheels are taken seriously (Villard de Honnecourt's drawing, Peregrinus' magnet wheel).
- **Weather instruments and forecasting** [`weather_instruments`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/weather_instruments.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept medium. Weather is foretold from stars, almanacs and country signs. Weathercocks show wind; nobody measures humidity, rain or wind strength. Elsewhere: Oxford, William Merle's daily weather record (1337-1344); China, rain and snow gauges.
- **Spherical Earth and its size** [`round_earth_size`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/round_earth_size.md) — K4, use partial, make easy, accept high. Every educated Florentine knows the sphere from Sacrobosco and Dante. The size follows Alfraganus (20,400 miles); Ptolemy's Geography is unknown in Latin. Local: Dante's Commedia and Convivio; Restoro d'Arezzo's vernacular Composizione del mondo (1282).
- **Cause of the seasons (tilted axis)** [`seasons_axial_tilt`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/seasons_axial_tilt.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Taught correctly as the obliquity of the Sun's path (Sacrobosco), but with the Sun circling a fixed Earth.
- **Cause and prediction of eclipses** [`eclipse_prediction`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/eclipse_prediction.md) — K3, use correct, make medium, accept high. Causes are understood. Predictions from the Toledan Tables or the new Alfonsine Tables can be off by an hour or more; astrologers compute them. Local: Paolo dell'Abbaco; astrologers. Elsewhere: Paris, John of Saxony and Jean de Murs (Alfonsine Tables); Oxford, Merton astronomers.
- **Heliocentric model** [`heliocentrism`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/heliocentrism.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept low. Unheard of; schoolmen at most debate whether the Earth could turn daily. The Inquisition burned the astrologer Cecco d'Ascoli in Florence in 1327. Local: Franciscan inquisitor at Santa Croce.
